content: The postpartum period is often associated with maternal complications, including psychological and mental health issues, as well as neonatal morbidity. These complications can become chronic and have long-term consequences if not addressed. Home visits by healthcare professionals or trained lay supporters during the early postpartum weeks may help mitigate these risks. This review, updated from its 2017 version, evaluates the effects of different home-visiting schedules on maternal and newborn outcomes during the early postpartum period. The primary aim of this review was to assess how variations in home-visiting schedules—such as the number of visits, timing (e.g., within 48 hours of birth), duration, intensity (visits per week), and type of intervention—affect maternal and neonatal mortality. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that enrolled participants within 42 days postpartum. Studies involving antenatal interventions or those focusing exclusively on high-risk groups (e.g., women with substance use disorders) were excluded. The review included 16 RCTs involving 12,080 women from both highand low-resource settings. In low-resource settings, usual care often meant no additional postnatal care after early hospital discharge. The interventions varied widely, but most were delivered by healthcare professionals and aimed to assess maternal and neonatal well-being, provide education, and offer support. Some interventions had specific goals, such as promoting breastfeeding or providing practical assistance. However, the evidence was inconsistent, and many studies had a high or unclear risk of bias. Key Findings: 1. More vs. Fewer Home Visits (5 studies, 2102 women): The evidence is very uncertain regarding the impact of home visits on maternal and neonatal mortality (very low-certainty evidence). Postnatal depression scores, measured using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS), may be slightly worse with more home visits, but the difference was not clinically significant (mean difference [MD] 1.02, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.25 to 1.79; low-certainty evidence). Maternal satisfaction showed conflicting results. One analysis suggested a potential benefit with fewer visits (risk ratio [RR] 0.96, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.02; low-certainty evidence), while another study found increased satisfaction with additional support from health visitors (MD 14.70, 95% CI 8.43 to 20.97; low-certainty evidence). More home visits may reduce infant healthcare utilization (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.64; low-certainty evidence) and increase exclusive breastfeeding rates at six weeks (RR 1.17, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.36; low-certainty evidence). Serious neonatal morbidity up to six months was not reported in any trial. 2. Different Models of Postnatal Care (3 studies, 4394 women): In a cluster-RCT comparing usual care with individualized care by midwives extended up to three months postpartum, there may be little to no difference in neonatal mortality (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.12). Individualized care probably reduces the proportion of women with EPDS scores ≥ 13 at four months (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.86). One study found little to no difference between home visits and telephone screening in neonatal morbidity up to 28 days (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.12). Another study found no difference between breastfeeding promotion and routine visits in exclusive breastfeeding rates at six months (RR 1.47, 95% CI 0.81 to 2.69). 3. Home vs. Facility-Based Postnatal Care (8 studies, 5179 women): There may be little to no difference in postnatal depression rates at 42 days postpartum or as measured on the EPDS scale at 60 days. Maternal satisfaction with postnatal care may be higher with home visits (RR 1.36, 95% CI 1.14 to 1.62; low-certainty evidence). There may be little to no difference in infant emergency healthcare visits or hospital readmissions (RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.38) or in exclusive breastfeeding rates at two weeks (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.18). Authors' Conclusions: The evidence regarding the impact of home visits on maternal and neonatal mortality is highly uncertain. Individualized care as part of a home-visiting package likely improves maternal depression scores at four months postpartum. Increasing the frequency of home visits may enhance exclusive breastfeeding rates and reduce infant healthcare utilization. Maternal satisfaction with postnatal care may also be higher with home visits compared to facility-based care. However, the overall certainty of the evidence is low, and findings were inconsistent across studies. Further well-designed RCTs are needed to determine the optimal home-visiting schedule and intervention package.
